money_at_stake.rationale: No aggregate budget figure for Japan's national civil defence shelter program has been published, and this occurrence is about that program, not about the single Yaesu car park alone: the card's own framing is a national procurement chain behind roughly 1,500 identified sites, and one car park is not a fair proxy for that. A Japanese business-analysis site states the gap in as many words as of 2026-06-23: the specific amount for shelter development itself has not been disclosed, and it explicitly separates this from Japan's much larger, unrelated National Resilience program (roughly 20 trillion yen over five years for earthquake and flood infrastructure, not shelters). The one hard number found anywhere is a single-site figure: about 4.2 billion yen allocated for the comparable 1,400 square metre Azabu-Juban conversion, versus the Yaesu site's roughly 13,000 square metres. Scaling that one number into a national band with no disclosed funding formula or multiplier would be exactly the reasoned-but-unsourced estimate this leg forbids. The same reporting states there is currently no national funding mechanism for shelter construction, so individual municipalities bear most of the cost themselves, which argues against inferring one clean national figure at all. Market-size guesses circulating on Japanese retail-investing blogs (roughly 2 trillion yen to refit all identified sites nationwide, or roughly 10 trillion yen for 10 million people of capacity at an assumed per-person cost) are unattributed to any government or primary source and are the SPECULATIVE number this leg exists to refuse rather than adopt.
money_at_stake.basis: Searched the Cabinet Secretariat's 2026-03-31 basic policy on securing shelters, English-language coverage (SCMP, Japan Times, Global Construction Review, trade.gov), and Japanese financial and industry commentary (Nikkei, Jiji, resilience-biz-navi, kabukiso). No outlet ties a dated, sourced aggregate spending figure to the national shelter program specifically; one secondary source states outright that the specific amount has not been disclosed. The only concrete figure found is a single-site cost (about 4.2 billion yen for one 1,400 sqm conversion), which cannot stand in for the national program without an unsupported extrapolation, so the leg is recorded NULL rather than banded from that one data point.

public_reach.rationale: Real, named, listed exposure exists, but it is a fragmented set of small-caps plus one large-cap whose exposure is immaterial to its own group economics, which is squarely the 'mixed' anchor rather than the 'pure-plays carry most of it' anchor. A dated Japanese finance site's 'nuclear shelter related stocks' list names seven Tokyo Stock Exchange listed companies with disclosed shelter-relevant product lines: Sanyo Homes (1420, residential shelter rooms), Giken Holdings (1443, radiation and electromagnetic shielding construction), SE Corp (3423, ESCON high-strength fibre-reinforced concrete for disaster-resistant structures), Nippon Filcon (5942, radiation-shielding concrete via its Gcon line), Daikin Industries (6367, ventilation and filtration equipment), Nippon Tungsten (6998, tungsten radiation-shielding sheets), and Press Kogyo (7246, evacuation shelter products). Separately, ITOKI Corporation (7972, TSE listed) has a purpose-built blast door for underground civil-defence shelters, confirmed directly on the company's own newsroom page. That is a genuine, if fragmented, slate of named listed issuers already tied to this exact theme by name, which is stronger evidence than an unnamed general claim that 'contractors are listed.' Not scored higher because the largest name in the set, Daikin, is a huge diversified global HVAC conglomerate for which shelter-related ventilation work is immaterial to group earnings, and because the bulk of physical digging and retrofit construction work for a program like this typically runs through general contractors who are not yet confirmed by name for this specific program.

capture_odds.rationale: Genuinely mixed, so scored near the middle rather than rounded toward either story. For capture: the named suppliers hold narrow technical niches (radiation-shielding concrete and sheet products, purpose-built blast doors, high-strength fibre-reinforced concrete) that are not commodity building materials, which is the structural shape that can hold pricing power. Against capture: procurement looks diffuse rather than programmatic. There is no disclosed national funding mechanism, so individual municipalities fund most of the work themselves, which historically means many small, separately-negotiated local tenders rather than one large program run by a single well-resourced buyer able to pay a premium for scarce capability. The listed set is also thin relative to the likely number of unlisted specialist subcontractors and general contractors doing the bulk of physical construction, and the one large diversified name in the set (Daikin) would feel no material earnings effect even from fast growth in shelter-related ventilation revenue, since it is a small line inside a global HVAC business.

timing_fit.rationale: Rescored down from 60 after the Japan Times citation for the Yaesu-specific survey timeline could not be verified this run: the source returned HTTP 402 Payment Required, and no Wayback Machine snapshot could be fetched either (web.archive.org is unreachable from this environment), so that evidence item is deleted rather than kept on a page nobody opened this run, per the source_excerpt procedure. What survives is the Cabinet's own dated basic policy (2026-03-31, confirmed as this article's publication date on refetch): a national target to secure enough emergency shelters to cover all residents at the municipal level by 2030, raised from a prefectural-level target the policy itself says is already on track to be met in fiscal 2026. That is still credible-inside-window evidence that the underlying national program's money moves inside the 2 to 5 year horizon (2030 sits about 3.4 years from this appraisal's as_of date), which keeps the score close to the prior 60 anchor rather than dropping toward 'slipping past it'. It sits a notch below the prior score because the surviving evidence speaks to the national program's own timeline, not to the Yaesu site specifically, and the site-level near-term catalyst (the survey Governor Koike announced for the fiscal year through March) can no longer be attributed to a source this run actually opened; independent WebSearch results (Japan Today, SCMP) still corroborate that announcement happened, but a search snippet is not a citable evidence item under this stage's own rule.

notes.text: Independently verified Nell's dated occurrence claim before appraising it: Japan Times (2026-08-08) and SCMP corroborate Governor Koike's Yaesu survey announcement, the roughly 13,000 sqm floor area, the 2 to 11 metre depth, blast-proof doors and emergency-supply storage, and the Azabu-Juban precedent. No discrepancy found; the claim holds as written.

UNRANKED here is not a comment on whether this occurrence is worth a chain build. public_reach (60), capture_odds (45) and timing_fit (55) are all scored and none is weak; the entire gap is that nobody, including the Japanese government itself, has published what the national shelter program actually costs. That is itself the finding Nell's card asked this appraisal to produce ('the money size is the open question and that is Tally's'): it is genuinely open, not quietly large or quietly small. A re-run should re-check for a published figure after Japan's next budget cycle, since 90 days from now (review_by 2026-11-28) sits inside the window where a FY2027 budget request could disclose a shelter-specific line item.
